procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated February 26, 1965 of the Madras High Court in Writ Petitions Nos. 1321, 1456, 1495, 1496 and 1553 of 1964.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: Respondents filed writ petitions in the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution challenging the search and seizure of their premises by the Department of the appellant. The High Court concluded that the search was defective because safeguards in s. 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not followed. The High Court also held that sub-sections (2), (3), and (4) of section 41 were unconstitutional as they were unreasonable restrictions on fundamental rights guaranteed under Art. 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution. In one petition, the High Court found the search warrant was defective because the magistrate had not applied his mind to the necessity of the search.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State Government appealed the High Court's decision based on certificates granted by the Madras High Court. The State Government argued that s.41 authorized the search and seizure, that the State Legislature was competent to enact s.41(4), and that the provisions did not offend Art. 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution.

directions: Parties to bear their own costs in all the appeals.

issue.issue_text: Whether Section 41(2) of the Act confers the power of search or is limited to the power of inspection.

facts: The High Court had previously ruled that Section 41(2) of the Act only provided for the power of inspection and did not include the power of search, viewing them as two distinct actions.
law: Section 41(2) provides that a dealer's accounts, records, goods, offices, shops, godowns, and vehicles shall be open to inspection.
The Court acknowledged the general principle that a power to inspect does not necessarily give the power to search.
application: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court's narrow interpretation.
It reasoned that Section 41(2) grants multiple powers of inspection: (i) of accounts and documents, (ii) of goods, and (iii) of the dealer's business premises (offices, shops, etc.).
The Court argued that when the power to inspect premises is combined with the power to inspect the items within those premises (like accounts and goods), it effectively amounts to a power of search.

The Court explained that the only logical purpose for an officer to enter a shop for 'inspection' is to find the accounts and goods to be inspected. This act of looking for items within the premises is functionally a search.

Therefore, even though the word 'search' is not explicitly used, the combination of these inspection powers implicitly grants the authority to enter and search the business premises to find the relevant documents and goods.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was wrong. It held that the combined powers granted under Section 41(2) to inspect both the business premises and the accounts/goods within them effectively confer the power of search.

issue.issue_text: Whether sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 41 are unconstitutional on the ground of being unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property and to carry on trade.

law.name: Constitution of India, Art. 19(1)(f) & (g)
law.description: Guarantees the fundamental rights to hold property and to carry on any trade or business. These rights can be subjected to reasonable restrictions.

application.detail: The Supreme Court disagreed with the High Court and found that the provisions contained sufficient safeguards to be considered reasonable restrictions.

Regarding sub-section (3) (seizure of accounts), the Court identified several safeguards: (1) the officer must have a reason to suspect tax evasion; (2) reasons must be recorded in writing before the seizure; (3) a receipt must be given to the dealer for the seized items; (4) accounts can only be retained for as long as necessary for examination; and (5) there is a 30-day time limit on retention, which can only be extended with permission from a higher officer.
application.implication: These procedural requirements prevent arbitrary action and ensure the power is not misused, making the restriction on property rights reasonable.

application.detail: Regarding sub-section (2) (power of search), the Court held that the power was not arbitrary. It found that safeguards provided in the Code of Criminal Procedure apply to searches conducted under this sub-section.
application.implication: By incorporating established legal safeguards for searches, the law ensures that the restriction on the right to carry on trade is not unreasonable, especially given its objective of preventing tax evasion.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that due to the presence of these multiple safeguards in both sub-sections, the restrictions imposed on the right to hold property and carry on trade were reasonable and not unconstitutional. The Court, therefore, rejected the challenge to the constitutionality of sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 41.

issue.issue_text: Whether the search of the residential accommodation was illegal due to the magistrate's non-application of mind in issuing the warrant.

facts: A search warrant for a residential house was issued by a magistrate using a pre-printed form.
law: A magistrate must apply their mind to the necessity of a search before issuing a warrant.
application: The Supreme Court noted the High Court's finding that the magistrate had not applied their mind when issuing the warrant.
The evidence for this non-application of mind was that the magistrate had failed to strike out irrelevant portions of the printed form and had not filled in necessary gaps before issuing it.
These omissions indicated that the warrant was issued mechanically, without proper consideration.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's conclusion, referring to the warrant as "defective." Consequently, it ordered that anything recovered from the search of the residential accommodation conducted on the basis of this invalid warrant must be returned.

issue.issue_text: Whether the search was defective for non-compliance with the safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.

facts: A search was conducted where authorities seized accounts and other items.

The authorities conducting the search, as well as the High Court, operated under the assumption that the provisions of Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) did not apply to this type of search.
law: The proviso to sub-section (2) of the relevant act mandates that all searches conducted under it shall, as far as may be, be made in accordance with the provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
The Supreme Court held that this proviso makes the safeguards contained in Section 165 of the Cr.P.C. applicable to these searches, 'mutatis mutandis' (with necessary changes).

These safeguards include: (i) the officer must have reasonable grounds for belief, (ii) believe the item cannot be obtained otherwise without undue delay, (iii) record the grounds of belief in writing, and (iv) specify the thing for which the search is being made.
application: The Court found that the safeguards provided under Section 165 of the Cr.P.C. were not followed when the search was made.
The reason for this non-compliance was the mistaken belief by all parties involved that Section 165 was not applicable to the search.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that because the mandatory safeguards of Section 165 of the Cr.P.C. were not followed, the search was defective. Consequently, anything recovered as a result of this defective search must be returned.

issue.issue_text: Whether sub-section (4) of Section 41, which provides for seizure and confiscation, is valid.

facts: The validity of sub-section (4) of Section 41 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, which authorized the seizure and confiscation of goods, was challenged.
The High Court had previously struck down this sub-section, finding it was beyond the legislative competence of the State.
Sub-section (4) contained a second proviso, added by a 1961 amendment, which included a clause (a).
law: A provision within a statute can be struck down if it is found to be repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act.
The doctrine of severability determines whether an invalid part of a statute can be removed while leaving the rest of the statute intact.
If an invalid provision is not severable, the entire section or statute it is part of must be struck down.
application: The Supreme Court agreed with the High Court's conclusion to strike down sub-section (4), but for entirely different reasons.

The Court's reasoning focused on clause (a) of the second proviso to sub-section (4). It found this clause to be "repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act" because it provided for the recovery of tax even before the taxable event (the first sale in the State) had occurred.
The Court then considered whether this repugnant proviso could be severed, leaving the main part of sub-section (4) in force.

It concluded that the proviso was not severable. The Court reasoned that because the legislature added this compulsory proviso at a later date, it clearly intended for the main part of the section and the proviso to operate together.
Therefore, the Court found it could not hold that the legislature intended for the main part of sub-section (4) to stand by itself without the proviso.
reasoning.conclusion: Because the repugnant second proviso was not severable from the main part of the sub-section, the Supreme Court held that the entire sub-section (4), along with its provisos, must fall and be struck down.

arguments.issue_text: Whether Section 41(2) of the Act confers the power of search or is limited to the power of inspection.
appellant_arguments: Section 41 of the Act authorises search and seizure.
respondent_arguments: The power under Section 41(2) is limited to inspection and does not include the power to search.

arguments.issue_text: Whether sub-sections (2) and (3) of Section 41 are unconstitutional on the ground of being unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property and to carry on trade.
appellant_arguments: The provisions do not violate Article 19(1)(f) and (g) of the Constitution and are protected as reasonable restrictions under Article 19(5) and (6).
respondent_arguments: Sub-sections (2) and (3) are unconstitutional as they impose unreasonable restrictions on the right to hold property and to carry on trade.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the search of the residential accommodation was illegal due to the magistrate's non-application of mind in issuing the warrant.
appellant_arguments: The search and the warrant on which it was based were legal and valid.
respondent_arguments: The search was illegal because it was based on a defective warrant issued without proper application of mind by the magistrate.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the search was defective for non-compliance with the safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure.
appellant_arguments: The safeguards under Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not applicable to a search conducted under Section 41(2) of the Act.
respondent_arguments: The search was defective because the mandatory safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not followed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether sub-section (4) of Section 41, which provides for seizure and confiscation, is valid.
appellant_arguments: The power to seize and confiscate goods is ancillary and incidental to the power to tax under item 54, List II, and is necessary to check tax evasion.
The State Legislature was competent to enact sub-section (4).
respondent_arguments: The power of confiscation in sub-section (4) was beyond the legislative competence of the State Legislature under item 54, List II.

cases.case_name: State of Rajasthan v. Leela Jain
cases.principle: For the general principle of construction that the function of a proviso is to limit the main part of the section and carve out something which but for the proviso would be within the main part.

cases.case_name: Blwndda Urban District Council v. Taff Vale Railway Co.
cases.principle: For the broad general rule of construction that a section or enactment must be construed as a whole, each portion throwing light, if need be, on the rest.

cases.case_name: Commissioner of Income-tax v. Nandlal Bhandari & Sons
cases.principle: For the principle that the sound interpretation and meaning of a statute is to prevail, based on a view of the enacting clause, saving clause, and proviso, taken and construed together.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A statutory power of search is not an unreasonable restriction on fundamental rights if it incorporates procedural safeguards, such as those in the Code of Criminal Procedure; however, any search conducted without adhering to these incorporated safeguards is defective, and anything recovered from it must be returned.
obiter: A section or enactment must be construed as a whole, with each part, including provisos, throwing light on the rest.
The substance of a proviso, not its form, determines whether it is an exception or a substantive provision.
A provision within a tax act that is repugnant to the general scheme of the act is invalid.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: While the Court upheld the constitutional validity of the power to search premises and seize account books under Section 41(2) and (3) of the Act as a reasonable restriction necessary to prevent tax evasion, it ultimately dismissed the state's appeal. The specific searches conducted were deemed illegal because the search of the residential accommodation was based on a defective warrant and the general search failed to comply with the mandatory procedural safeguards of Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Furthermore, the Court struck down the power of confiscation in Section 41(4) as it was repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act.
legal_tests_applied: Reasonable Restriction Test: The court assessed whether the restrictions imposed by the law on the fundamental rights under Article 19(1)(f) and (g) were reasonable and in the public interest, specifically considering the objective of preventing tax evasion and the presence of procedural safeguards.
why_appellant_lost: The search of the residential accommodation was illegal because it was conducted on the basis of a defective warrant, requiring the return of anything recovered.

The search of the business premises was defective because the mandatory safeguards provided in Section 165 of the Code of Criminal Procedure were not followed, which the court held were applicable to searches under Section 41(2) of the Act.

The court struck down sub-section (4) of Section 41, which provided for confiscation, finding it repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act because it compelled the recovery of tax before the taxable event (the first point of sale) had occurred.
why_respondent_won: The court agreed that the search was illegal because it was based on a defective warrant, stating: 'anything recovered from the search of the residential accommodation on the basis of this defective warrant must be· returned.'

The court found that the search was vitiated by non-compliance with mandatory procedures, reasoning: 'as the safeguards provided in s. 165 of the Code of Crimina I Procedure were not followed, anything recovered on a defective search of this kind must be returned.'
The court invalidated the confiscation provision, holding: 'As such it was repugnant to the entire scheme of the Act and sub-section (4) must therefore be struck down.'
policy_considerations: The necessity of granting search and seizure powers in taxation laws to effectively check tax evasion is a valid legislative objective.

The power to search, even if valid, must be constrained by procedural safeguards to prevent it from becoming arbitrary. The incorporation of safeguards from the Code of Criminal Procedure makes the restriction on rights reasonable.

The government is expected to exercise its power to authorize officers for searches responsibly by empowering officers of proper status. The mere existence of the power to authorize any officer does not make the law unconstitutional.
